name: Pancreatic cancer
definition: Pancreatic cancer is a cancer that starts in the pancreas, an organ that helps with digestion.
overview: Pancreatic cancer often causes no symptoms at first, and when symptoms appear they can be vague. The NHS says it can be difficult to treat. Known risk factors include smoking, long-term diabetes, chronic pancreatitis and certain hereditary disorders, although many people with risk factors never develop it. Treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and when a cure is not possible the focus is on controlling symptoms.
causes: Doctors do not know exactly what causes pancreatic cancer
Risk factors such as smoking and long-term diabetes are linked to it, but many people with them never develop the cancer
riskFactors: Certain hereditary disorders and a family history of the disease
Older age, with one NHS source listing age over 65
signs: Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice)
Changes to stools or bowel habits
complications: A blocked bile duct, causing jaundice
Reduced production of digestive enzymes, which can lead to malnutrition
Spread of the cancer to other parts of the body
diagnosis: Diagnosis typically combines a physical examination, blood tests, imaging and a biopsy, which is a sample of tissue. Doctors use information from several tests, along with symptoms and medical history. NICE guidance recommends a CT scan using a pancreatic protocol as the first scan for suspected pancreatic cancer. If the diagnosis is still unclear, a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both may be offered.
treatment: Treatment depends on the size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread and the person's general health. Surgery is used to remove the cancer when it can be removed, and to relieve symptoms such as jaundice or blockages when it cannot. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are also used, and targeted therapy is another option. Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms such as pain, tiredness, nausea and digestion problems.
prevention: Smoking is a risk factor that can be changed. Pancreatic Cancer UK says the UK has no screening programme, although people with a family history may be monitored.
seekCare: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for yellowing of the skin or eyes. Pancreatic Cancer UK says jaundice needs a GP or A&E straight away. A GP appointment is advised for noticeable weight loss without trying or other symptoms that last longer than two weeks. Having these symptoms does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of pancreatic cancer?
sections.body:
The NHS says pancreatic cancer may not cause any symptoms, or the symptoms may be hard to spot. MedlinePlus says early pancreatic cancer often does not cause symptoms right away, and that when symptoms appear they are often vague.

Yellowing of the skin or eyes, called jaundice, is one of the common signs. The NHS also lists loss of appetite, losing weight without trying and tiredness. Digestive symptoms include nausea and changes in bowel habits, and the NHS describes upper abdominal pain that may ease when leaning forward. Cancer Research UK lists tummy or back pain and changes to stools among the common symptoms. Pancreatic Cancer UK adds indigestion and recently diagnosed diabetes, while Macmillan also lists feeling very tired and feeling bloated after meals.

Many of these symptoms have other causes. The NHS notes that having them does not definitely mean a person has pancreatic cancer.

sections.heading: What causes pancreatic cancer, and who is at higher risk?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says doctors do not know what causes pancreatic cancer. Known risk factors include smoking, long-term diabetes, chronic pancreatitis and certain hereditary disorders. Some risk factors, such as smoking, can be changed, while others, such as genetics and family history, cannot. Many people with risk factors never develop pancreatic cancer, while some people with no known risk factors do.

Other NHS-affiliated pages list being overweight or obese and being over 65 as factors that can raise the risk. The Royal Marsden page also lists heavy drinking and a high intake of red or processed meat. Pancreatic Cancer UK says there is no screening programme for pancreatic cancer in the UK, although people with a family history may be monitored.

sections.heading: How is pancreatic cancer diagnosed?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says diagnosis typically combines a physical examination, blood tests, imaging and a biopsy. Doctors use information from several tests, together with the symptoms and medical history.

NICE guidance recommends a CT scan using a pancreatic protocol for people with suspected pancreatic cancer, including before the bile duct is drained in people with jaundice caused by a blockage. If the diagnosis is still unclear, NICE says a PET-CT scan, an endoscopic ultrasound or both may be offered. A published review describes endoscopic ultrasound with a fine-needle biopsy as the standard way of establishing the diagnosis. A CT-guided biopsy can be an alternative when endoscopic ultrasound is unsuitable or unavailable, mainly for tumours that cannot be removed.

Cancer Research UK says a procedure called ERCP can help confirm the diagnosis by taking samples from abnormal areas. The same procedure can be used to place a small tube, called a stent, in a blocked bile duct.

sections.heading: How is pancreatic cancer treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says pancreatic cancer can be difficult to treat. The options depend on the size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread and the person's general health. Surgery is used to remove the cancer when it can be removed, and also to relieve symptoms such as jaundice or blockages when it cannot. The National Cancer Institute says surgery is only potentially curative when the tumour can be removed.

The National Cancer Institute describes chemotherapy as the main treatment once the cancer has spread, and says it can sometimes shrink the tumour or help people live longer. The NHS lists chemotherapy and radiotherapy among the treatments used. MedlinePlus also lists targeted therapy as an option.

sections.heading: Living with pancreatic cancer and managing symptoms
sections.body:
For many people it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer. In those cases the main aim is often to control symptoms, and palliative treatment can improve quality of life by easing the symptoms and complications of the disease. Macmillan says palliative care doctors and nurses specialise in symptom control and supportive care, and that a GP or specialist can refer a person to a palliative team.

The NHS says supportive care covers issues such as digestion problems, pain, tiredness and nausea. The National Cancer Institute explains that removing part of the pancreas can reduce its ability to make digestive enzymes, so replacement enzymes may be prescribed to prevent malnutrition.

A blocked bile duct causes jaundice, and a stent can keep the duct open so that bile drains. If a stent is not suitable, bypass surgery is an alternative, and medication can ease the itching that jaundice may cause.

faqs.a: For many people it will not be possible to cure pancreatic cancer, and the main aim of treatment is then often to control symptoms. The National Cancer Institute says surgery is only potentially curative when the tumour can be removed. The NHS says the options depend on the size and position of the cancer, whether it has spread and the person's general health.

faqs.q: Does pancreatic cancer always cause symptoms?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says pancreatic cancer may not have any symptoms, or they may be hard to spot. MedlinePlus says early pancreatic cancer often does not cause symptoms right away, and that symptoms are often vague when they appear. Many of the symptoms also have other causes.

faqs.q: Is there a screening test for pancreatic cancer?
faqs.a: Pancreatic Cancer UK says the UK has no screening programme for pancreatic cancer. It adds that people with a family history may be monitored. MedlinePlus lists hereditary disorders and family history among the risk factors that cannot be changed.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about possible symptoms?
faqs.a: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for yellowing of the skin or eyes. It advises a GP appointment for noticeable weight loss without trying or for symptoms that last longer than two weeks. Pancreatic Cancer UK says jaundice needs a GP or A&E straight away.
